Lipschitz clustering in normed spaces
and barycentric spaces

Leonid V. Kovalev
Abstract.

For every normed space XX and integers 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, we construct a Lipschitz retraction from X⁡(n)X(n) onto X⁡(k)X(k) with constant at most 2+8​n​(n−1)2+8n(n-1), independently of the dimension of XX. Here X⁡(n)X(n) consists of the nonempty subsets of XX with at most nn points, equipped with the Hausdorff metric. For the consecutive case k=n−1k=n-1, a separate construction gives the sharper asymptotic bound O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n). These results extend to barycentric metric spaces and settle some open problems on Lipschitz retractions.

Key words and phrases: 
Finite subset space, normed space, Lipschitz retraction, barycenter, clustering, absolute Lipschitz retract
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 51F30; Secondary 46B20, 54B20, 54C15, 54E40

1. Introduction

Clustering reduces a finite configuration to a simpler one by merging nearby points. Its Lipschitz version asks that small perturbations of the input produce controlled perturbations of the output. We study retractions that reduce an nn-point configuration to at most kk representatives, where 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, and fix configurations already having at most kk points. Allowing fewer than kk representatives accommodates simultaneous mergers. Our main setting is that of normed spaces, with estimates independent of dimension.

For a metric space XX and an integer n≥1n\geq 1, write X⁡(n)={A⊂X:1≤|A|≤n}X(n)=\{A\subset X:1\leq|A|\leq n\}, with the Hausdorff metric

dH​(A,B)=max⁡{maxa∈A⁡minb∈B⁡d⁡(a,b),maxb∈B⁡mina∈A⁡d⁡(a,b)}.d_{H}(A,B)=\max\left\{\max_{a\in A}\min_{b\in B}d(a,b),\,\max_{b\in B}\min_{a\in A}d(a,b)\right\}.

Following [12], XX has the Lipschitz clustering property if there is a Lipschitz retraction X⁡(n)→X⁡(n−1)X(n)\to X(n-1) for every n≥2n\geq 2. For 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, set

Λn,k(X)=inf{Lip(r):r:X(n)→X(k) is a Lipschitz retraction},\Lambda_{n,k}(X)=\inf\{\Lip(r)\ :\ r\colon X(n)\to X(k)\text{ is a Lipschitz retraction}\},

with infimum +∞+\infty if no such retraction exists, and write Λn​(X)=Λn,n−1​(X)\Lambda_{n}(X)=\Lambda_{n,n-1}(X). If Λn​(X)<∞\Lambda_{n}(X)<\infty for all nn, composing consecutive retractions yields Λn,k​(X)<∞\Lambda_{n,k}(X)<\infty for all kk, but with weak quantitative control. Our first theorem avoids this by constructing r:X⁡(n)→X⁡(k)r\colon X(n)\to X(k) directly.

The Lipschitz clustering property was proved for Hilbert spaces in [11] and for Hadamard spaces in [4]. It also holds for finite-dimensional normed spaces: by John’s theorem, a normed space of dimension dd has Banach–Mazur distance at most d\sqrt{d} from ℓ2d\ell_{2}^{d}, so the Euclidean case applies, with constants that grow with dd. For arbitrary normed spaces, Akofor [1] obtained Lipschitz consecutive retractions for n=2,3n=2,3, and consecutive retractions that are Hölder continuous on bounded sets for general nn. He also proved the existence of Lipschitz retractions X⁡(n)→X⁡(1)X(n)\to X(1) and X⁡(n)→X⁡(2)X(n)\to X(2) for arbitrary n>2n>2 [1, Theorem 4.11]. The case of general normed spaces was posed as an open problem in [11, Question 3.4]; see also [12, §4], and [4, Remark 3.5] for strictly and uniformly convex spaces.

All normed spaces below are real, and completeness is not assumed; complex normed spaces are covered by regarding them as real spaces. We write conv⁡A\conv A for the convex hull of AA.

Theorem 1.1.

For every normed space XX and integers 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, there is a retraction r:X⁡(n)→X⁡(k)r\colon X(n)\to X(k) such that

Lip⁡(r)≤Dn:=2+8​n​(n−1),andr⁡(A)⊂conv⁡A​ for all ​A∈X⁡(n).\Lip(r)\leq D_{n}:=2+8n(n-1),\quad\text{and}\quad r(A)\subset\conv A\text{ for all }A\in X(n).

Moreover,

(1.1) dH​(r⁡(A),A)≤(n−1)​sk​(A),d_{H}(r(A),A)\leq(n-1)s_{k}(A),

where sk​(A)s_{k}(A) is the smallest s≥0s\geq 0 such that the graph on AA joining all pairs at distance at most ss has at most kk components (Definition 2.1).

For the consecutive case k=n−1k=n-1 a different construction achieves a Lipschitz constant of order O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n). Here and below, log\log denotes the natural logarithm.

Theorem 1.2.

For every normed space XX and every n≥2n\geq 2, there is a retraction r:X⁡(n)→X⁡(n−1)r\colon X(n)\to X(n-1) with

(1.2) Lip⁡(r)≤Cn:=1+48​n​log⁡(n+1),r⁡(A)⊂conv⁡A.\Lip(r)\leq C_{n}:=1+48n\log(n+1),\qquad r(A)\subset\conv A.

For n=2n=2, the midpoint retraction has Lipschitz constant one.

One has Cn<DnC_{n}<D_{n} exactly when n≥19n\geq 19, so for k=n−1k=n-1 Theorem 1.2 improves on Theorem 1.1 from n=19n=19 on. The order n​log⁡nn\log n is optimal up to the logarithm: every nonzero normed space satisfies Λn​(X)≥n−3\Lambda_{n}(X)\geq n-3 (Proposition 6.4, based on [2, Theorem 5.1]).

The construction in Theorem 1.1 harmonically interpolates the input vectors on their single-linkage tree and evaluates the interpolation at height sk​(A)s_{k}(A). The single-linkage hierarchy is the classical hierarchical clustering obtained from a minimum spanning tree [7, 9]. Carlsson and Mémoli [5] characterized it axiomatically, in contrast with Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem for flat clustering [10], and proved that it is stable under perturbations of the metric. This stability enters our proof through the fact that all merge heights move at most twice as fast as the input points. Lipschitz continuity of algorithms has recently been studied systematically in theoretical computer science, for example for minimum spanning trees [13].

For later use, set

(1.3) Bn,k=Dn(k≤n−2),Bn,n−1=min⁡{Dn,Cn}(n≥3),B2,1=1.B_{n,k}=D_{n}\quad(k\leq n-2),\qquad B_{n,n-1}=\min\{D_{n},C_{n}\}\quad(n\geq 3),\qquad B_{2,1}=1.

Thus Bn,n−1=DnB_{n,n-1}=D_{n} for 3≤n≤183\leq n\leq 18 and Bn,n−1=CnB_{n,n-1}=C_{n} for n≥19n\geq 19. By Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, and the midpoint map for n=2n=2, every normed space admits convex-hull-preserving retractions X⁡(n)→X⁡(k)X(n)\to X(k) with constant Bn,kB_{n,k}. All these constants are independent of dimension.

The above results have applications beyond normed spaces. Let 𝒫fin​(X)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X) be the finitely supported probability measures on a metric space XX, with the 11-Wasserstein distance W1W_{1}. A KK-Lipschitz barycenter (Definition 5.1) is a map β:𝒫fin​(X)→X\beta\colon\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X)\to X with β⁡(δx)=x\beta(\delta_{x})=x and d⁡(β⁡(μ),β⁡(ν))≤K​W1​(μ,ν)d(\beta(\mu),\beta(\nu))\leq KW_{1}(\mu,\nu).

Theorem 1.3.

If a metric space XX admits a KK-Lipschitz barycenter, then Λn,k​(X)≤K​Bn,k\Lambda_{n,k}(X)\leq KB_{n,k}, 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. Every complete metric space with a conical geodesic bicombing (Definition 5.6), including every complete Busemann-convex space and every Hadamard space, satisfies these bounds with K=1K=1.

This answers the questions in [4, Remark 3.5] concerning the improvement of the asymptotic Lipschitz bound for Hadamard spaces and the existence of such retractions in complete Busemann-convex spaces. For Hadamard spaces, Theorem 1.3 improves the consecutive retraction constant O⁡(n3/2)O(n^{3/2}) of [4] to O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n).

A separate construction (Theorem 2.3) gives Λn,k​(ℓ∞​(Γ))≤2​n−1\Lambda_{n,k}(\ell^{\infty}(\Gamma))\leq 2n-1 for 1≤k<n1\leq k<n and every index set Γ\Gamma, providing the sharp order of growth. Consequently, every absolute λ\lambda-Lipschitz retract (Definition 6.2) satisfies Λn,k≤λ⁡(2​n−1)\Lambda_{n,k}\leq\lambda(2n-1).

All Lipschitz constants between finite subset spaces refer to the Hausdorff metric. For labeled configurations we use the maximum of the distances between corresponding points. Section 2 gives efficient and explicit retractions between finite subset spaces of ℓ∞\ell^{\infty}; unfortunately, their output need not lie in the convex hull of the input. This short construction serves as a warm-up for Section 3, where Theorem 1.1 is proved. Section 4 proves Theorem 1.2. Section 5 concerns the applications of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 to metric spaces. Section 6 presents results for absolute Lipschitz retracts, lower bounds, and open questions.

2. Warm-up: clustering in ℓ∞\ell^{\infty}

In this section we construct an explicit (2​n−1)(2n-1)-Lipschitz retraction V⁡(n)→V⁡(k)V(n)\to V(k) for every 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, where V=ℓ∞​(Γ)V=\ell^{\infty}(\Gamma) and Γ\Gamma is an arbitrary nonempty index set. The construction is simpler than the one in Section 3 and shares some elements with it, such as the following definition.

Definition 2.1.

Let AA be a finite set with a pseudometric dd. For s≥0s\geq 0, let Gs​(A)G_{s}(A) be the graph with vertex set AA joining aa and bb whenever d⁡(a,b)≤sd(a,b)\leq s. For k≥1k\geq 1, the cut height of AA is

(2.1) sk​(A)=min⁡{s≥0:Gs​(A)​ has at most ​k​ components}.s_{k}(A)=\min\{s\geq 0:G_{s}(A)\text{ has at most }k\text{ components}\}.

If dd is a metric, then sk​(A)=0s_{k}(A)=0 exactly when |A|≤k|A|\leq k.

Lemma 2.2.

(a) If dd and d′d^{\prime} are pseudometrics on a finite set AA with |d⁡(a,b)−d′​(a,b)|≤η|d(a,b)-d^{\prime}(a,b)|\leq\eta for all a,b∈Aa,b\in A, then the cut heights of AA for dd and for d′d^{\prime} differ by at most η\eta.

(b) If AA and BB are finite subsets of a metric space, then |sk​(A)−sk​(B)|≤2​dH​(A,B)|s_{k}(A)-s_{k}(B)|\leq 2d_{H}(A,B).

Proof.

(a) Every edge of Gs​(A)G_{s}(A) for dd is an edge of Gs+η​(A)G_{s+\eta}(A) for d′d^{\prime}, so the latter graph has at most as many components. Hence the cut height for d′d^{\prime} is at most the cut height for dd plus η\eta, and symmetrically.

(b) Let ε=dH​(A,B)\varepsilon=d_{H}(A,B) and s=sk​(A)s=s_{k}(A), and choose a map f:A→Bf\colon A\to B with d⁡(a,f⁡(a))≤εd(a,f(a))\leq\varepsilon for all a∈Aa\in A. If aa and a′a^{\prime} are joined in Gs​(A)G_{s}(A), then f⁡(a)f(a) and f⁡(a′)f(a^{\prime}) are equal or joined in Gs+2​ε​(B)G_{s+2\varepsilon}(B). Every point of BB is within ε\varepsilon of some a∈Aa\in A, hence within 2​ε2\varepsilon of f⁡(a)f(a). Therefore Gs+2​ε​(B)G_{s+2\varepsilon}(B) has at most as many components as Gs​(A)G_{s}(A), that is, sk​(B)≤sk​(A)+2​εs_{k}(B)\leq s_{k}(A)+2\varepsilon. Interchange AA and BB to obtain |sk​(A)−sk​(B)|≤2​dH​(A,B)|s_{k}(A)-s_{k}(B)|\leq 2d_{H}(A,B). ∎

An isometric embedding of AA into ℓ∞​(Γ)\ell^{\infty}(\Gamma) provides a collection of 11-Lipschitz coordinate functions xγ:A→ℝx_{\gamma}\colon A\to\mathbb{R}, γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma, such that d⁡(a,b)=supγ∈Γ|xγ​(a)−xγ​(b)|d(a,b)=\sup_{\gamma\in\Gamma}|x_{\gamma}(a)-x_{\gamma}(b)| for all a,b∈Aa,b\in A. To replace AA by a smaller subset of ℓ∞​(Γ)\ell^{\infty}(\Gamma), we will modify the coordinate functions to make them constant on some subsets of AA.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2; all sets in the rest of this section have at most nn points.

For a finite set A⊂VA\subset V and s≥0s\geq 0, let ρA,s\rho_{A,s} be the shortest-path pseudometric on the complete graph with vertex set AA and edge lengths (∥a−b∥−s)+(\lVert a-b\rVert-s)^{+}. Then

∥a−b∥−(n−1)​s≤ρA,s​(a,b)≤∥a−b∥,\lVert a-b\rVert-(n-1)s\leq\rho_{A,s}(a,b)\leq\lVert a-b\rVert,

and the zero-distance classes of ρA,s\rho_{A,s} are exactly the components of Gs​(A)G_{s}(A). Define three maps from AA to VV as follows:

LA,s​(a)​(γ)=minz∈A⁡(z⁡(γ)+ρA,s​(a,z)),UA,s​(a)​(γ)=maxz∈A⁡(z⁡(γ)−ρA,s​(a,z)),L_{A,s}(a)(\gamma)=\min_{z\in A}\bigl(z(\gamma)+\rho_{A,s}(a,z)\bigr),\qquad U_{A,s}(a)(\gamma)=\max_{z\in A}\bigl(z(\gamma)-\rho_{A,s}(a,z)\bigr),

and YA,s​(a)=(LA,s​(a)+UA,s​(a))/2Y_{A,s}(a)=(L_{A,s}(a)+U_{A,s}(a))/2. Thus, for each coordinate γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma, the function a↦LA,s​(a)​(γ)a\mapsto L_{A,s}(a)(\gamma) is the largest function on AA that is 11-Lipschitz for ρA,s\rho_{A,s} and is majorized by coordinate evaluation a↦a⁡(γ)a\mapsto a(\gamma). Similarly, a↦UA,s​(a)​(γ)a\mapsto U_{A,s}(a)(\gamma) is the smallest such function that is minorized by the evaluation at γ\gamma. Since |z⁡(γ)−a⁡(γ)|≤∥a−z∥|z(\gamma)-a(\gamma)|\leq\lVert a-z\rVert, the bounds on ρA,s\rho_{A,s} give

a−(n−1)​s≤LA,s​(a)≤a≤UA,s​(a)≤a+(n−1)​sa-(n-1)s\leq L_{A,s}(a)\leq a\leq U_{A,s}(a)\leq a+(n-1)s

coordinatewise. Hence LA,s​(a)L_{A,s}(a) and UA,s​(a)U_{A,s}(a) are indeed elements of VV. Furthermore, ∥YA,s​(a)−a∥≤(n−1)​s/2\lVert Y_{A,s}(a)-a\rVert\leq(n-1)s/2, and LA,0​(a)=UA,0​(a)=aL_{A,0}(a)=U_{A,0}(a)=a. By the triangle inequality for ρA,s\rho_{A,s}, all three maps are constant on every zero-distance class, that is, on every component of Gs​(A)G_{s}(A).

Theorem 2.3.

The formula Rn,k​(A)={YA,sk​(A)​(a):a∈A}R_{n,k}(A)=\{Y_{A,s_{k}(A)}(a):a\in A\} defines a retraction V⁡(n)→V⁡(k)V(n)\to V(k) with Lip⁡(Rn,k)≤2​n−1\Lip(R_{n,k})\leq 2n-1.

Proof.

The output has at most as many points as Gsk​(A)​(A)G_{s_{k}(A)}(A) has components, hence at most kk. If |A|≤k|A|\leq k, then sk​(A)=0s_{k}(A)=0 and Rn,k​(A)=AR_{n,k}(A)=A. Given A,B∈V⁡(n)A,B\in V(n), let ε=dH​(A,B)\varepsilon=d_{H}(A,B), s=sk​(A)s=s_{k}(A) and t=sk​(B)t=s_{k}(B). By Lemma 2.2(b), |s−t|≤2​ε|s-t|\leq 2\varepsilon.

Given a,z∈Aa,z\in A and b,w∈Bb,w\in B with ∥a−b∥≤ε\lVert a-b\rVert\leq\varepsilon and ∥z−w∥≤ε\lVert z-w\rVert\leq\varepsilon, put c=2​ε+s−t≥0c=2\varepsilon+s-t\geq 0. If a≠za\neq z, choose a simple path a=a0,…,aq=za=a_{0},\ldots,a_{q}=z realizing ρA,s​(a,z)\rho_{A,s}(a,z), where q≤|A|−1≤n−1q\leq|A|-1\leq n-1. Choose bj∈Bb_{j}\in B with ∥aj−bj∥≤ε\lVert a_{j}-b_{j}\rVert\leq\varepsilon, taking b0=bb_{0}=b and bq=wb_{q}=w. For each edge,

(∥bj−bj−1∥−t)+≤(∥aj−aj−1∥−s)++c.(\lVert b_{j}-b_{j-1}\rVert-t)^{+}\leq(\lVert a_{j}-a_{j-1}\rVert-s)^{+}+c.

Summing gives

ρB,t​(b,w)≤ρA,s​(a,z)+(n−1)​(2​ε+s−t).\rho_{B,t}(b,w)\leq\rho_{A,s}(a,z)+(n-1)(2\varepsilon+s-t).

If a=za=z, the same inequality follows from

ρB,t​(b,w)≤(2​ε−t)+≤c≤(n−1)​c,\rho_{B,t}(b,w)\leq(2\varepsilon-t)^{+}\leq c\leq(n-1)c,

since ρA,s​(a,z)=0\rho_{A,s}(a,z)=0. Interchanging (A,s,a,z)(A,s,a,z) and (B,t,b,w)(B,t,b,w) gives

ρA,s​(a,z)≤ρB,t​(b,w)+(n−1)​(2​ε+t−s).\rho_{A,s}(a,z)\leq\rho_{B,t}(b,w)+(n-1)(2\varepsilon+t-s).

Since ∥a−b∥≤ε\lVert a-b\rVert\leq\varepsilon, these comparisons give coordinatewise inequalities

LB,t​(b)−LA,s​(a)≤ε+(n−1)​(2​ε+s−t),UB,t​(b)−UA,s​(a)≤ε+(n−1)​(2​ε+t−s).\begin{split}L_{B,t}(b)-L_{A,s}(a)&\leq\varepsilon+(n-1)(2\varepsilon+s-t),\\ U_{B,t}(b)-U_{A,s}(a)&\leq\varepsilon+(n-1)(2\varepsilon+t-s).\end{split}

Thus YB,t​(b)−YA,s​(a)≤(2​n−1)​εY_{B,t}(b)-Y_{A,s}(a)\leq(2n-1)\varepsilon coordinatewise. By symmetry, ∥YA,s​(a)−YB,t​(b)∥≤(2​n−1)​ε\lVert Y_{A,s}(a)-Y_{B,t}(b)\rVert\leq(2n-1)\varepsilon, and the theorem follows. ∎

3. Clustering by harmonic interpolation: proof of Theorem 1.1

3.1. Single-linkage trees and harmonic interpolation

For a finite metric space (A,d)(A,d), define

(3.1) uA​(a,b)=mina=a0,…,aq=b⁡max1≤j≤q⁡d⁡(aj−1,aj),uA​(a,a)=0.u_{A}(a,b)=\min_{a=a_{0},\ldots,a_{q}=b}\ \max_{1\leq j\leq q}d(a_{j-1},a_{j}),\qquad u_{A}(a,a)=0.

This is the single-linkage ultrametric [5, 7, 9]. A path realizing uAu_{A} may be taken simple, so if |A|=m|A|=m, then

(3.2) uA​(a,b)≤d⁡(a,b)≤(m−1)​uA​(a,b).u_{A}(a,b)\leq d(a,b)\leq(m-1)u_{A}(a,b).

The second inequality follows by summing the original distances along a simple minimizing path with at most m−1m-1 edges.

The components of the graph Gs​(A)G_{s}(A) of Definition 2.1 are the equivalence classes of the relation uA​(a,b)≤su_{A}(a,b)\leq s.

The nested components of graphs Gs​(A)G_{s}(A) form a rooted metric tree TAT_{A}. Its leaves are the points of AA, at height zero; the height h⁡(v)h(v) of a branching vertex vv is the threshold ss at which its children merge. An edge from a child vv to its parent p⁡(v)p(v) has length ℓv=h⁡(p⁡(v))−h⁡(v)\ell_{v}=h(p(v))-h(v). For two leaves a,ba,b, their least common ancestor has height uA​(a,b)u_{A}(a,b), and their tree distance is

(3.3) dTA​(a,b)=2​uA​(a,b).d_{T_{A}}(a,b)=2u_{A}(a,b).

For a finite rooted metric tree TT with leaves a1,…,ama_{1},\ldots,a_{m}, a function GG on its vertices, extended affinely along the edges, has Laplacian

Δ​G​(v)=∑w∼vG⁡(v)−G⁡(w)ℓv​w\Delta G(v)=\sum_{w\sim v}\frac{G(v)-G(w)}{\ell_{vw}}

at each nonleaf vertex vv. Thus −Δ​G​(v)-\Delta G(v) is the sum of the slopes of GG along the edges leaving vv. We call GG harmonic if Δ​G=0\Delta G=0 at every nonleaf vertex. This definition applies equally to vector-valued functions. Given boundary (vector) values x1,…,xm∈Xx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in X, the harmonic interpolation F:T→XF\colon T\to X is affine on each edge, takes value xix_{i} at aia_{i}, and satisfies

(3.4) Δ​F​(v)=∑w∼vF⁡(v)−F⁡(w)ℓv​w=0\Delta F(v)=\sum_{w\sim v}\frac{F(v)-F(w)}{\ell_{vw}}=0

at every nonleaf vertex vv, including the root. By (3.4), F⁡(v)F(v) is a weighted average of adjacent values, which yields the maximum principle in the scalar-valued case. The maximum principle gives uniqueness of solution, and therefore its existence, since the matrix of (3.4) is square [14, §2.1]. For a leaf aia_{i}, let ω⋅​(i)\omega_{\cdot}(i) be the scalar solution equal to 11 at aia_{i} and to 00 at the other leaves. Thus ωv​(i)\omega_{v}(i) is the harmonic measure of aia_{i} with respect to vv. The maximum principle gives ωv​(i)≥0\omega_{v}(i)\geq 0, and we have ∑iωv​(i)=1\sum_{i}\omega_{v}(i)=1 because constants are harmonic. We obtain the unique solution of (3.4), in any vector space XX, via the formula

(3.5) F⁡(v)=∑iωv​(i)​xi∈conv⁡{x1,…,xm}.F(v)=\sum_{i}\omega_{v}(i)x_{i}\in\conv\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\}.
Lemma 3.1 (Edge slopes).

Let TT be a finite rooted tree with m≥2m\geq 2 leaves, with heights as above: leaves at height zero and edge lengths given by height differences. Let FF be the harmonic interpolation of boundary vectors satisfying

∥xi−xj∥≤L​dT​(ai,aj).\lVert x_{i}-x_{j}\rVert\leq L\,d_{T}(a_{i},a_{j}).

For a nonroot vertex vv, let

Dv​F=F⁡(v)−F⁡(p⁡(v))ℓvD_{v}F=\frac{F(v)-F(p(v))}{\ell_{v}}

be the slope of FF on the edge from p⁡(v)p(v) down to vv, and let CvC_{v} be the set of leaves descending from vv. Put qi=Dai​Fq_{i}=D_{a_{i}}F. If vv is an ancestor of aia_{i}, then

(3.6) ∥F⁡(v)−xi∥≤2​L​h​(v).\lVert F(v)-x_{i}\rVert\leq 2Lh(v).

Moreover, ∥qi∥≤2​L\lVert q_{i}\rVert\leq 2L,

(3.7) Dv​F=∑i∈Cvqi,∑iqi=0,D_{v}F=\sum_{i\in C_{v}}q_{i},\qquad\sum_{i}q_{i}=0,

and ∥Dv​F∥≤2​L​⌊m/2⌋\lVert D_{v}F\rVert\leq 2L\lfloor m/2\rfloor for every nonroot vertex vv.

Proof.

Fix a leaf aia_{i}. Write v∧aiv\wedge a_{i} for the least common ancestor of vv and aia_{i}, and consider the function gi​(v)=2​h​(v∧ai)g_{i}(v)=2h(v\wedge a_{i}). On the root-to-aia_{i} path this function has slope 22 in the upward direction; it is constant on every branch off that path. Hence Δ​gi=0\Delta g_{i}=0 at all nonleaf vertices except the root, where Δ​gi=2\Delta g_{i}=2. Its boundary values are gi​(aj)=dT​(ai,aj)g_{i}(a_{j})=d_{T}(a_{i},a_{j}).

For every functional φ∈X∗\varphi\in X^{*} with ∥φ∥≤1\lVert\varphi\rVert\leq 1, the function G=φ⁡(F−xi)−L​giG=\varphi(F-x_{i})-Lg_{i} satisfies Δ​G≤0\Delta G\leq 0 at the nonleaf vertices, that is, G⁡(w)G(w) is at most the weighted average of the adjacent values. For v=p⁡(ai)v=p(a_{i}) it gives ∥qi∥=∥xi−F⁡(p⁡(ai))∥/h⁡(p⁡(ai))≤2​L\lVert q_{i}\rVert=\lVert x_{i}-F(p(a_{i}))\rVert/h(p(a_{i}))\leq 2L.

In Δ​F​(v)\Delta F(v), the edge above vv contributes Dv​FD_{v}F, and each edge below vv contributes minus its slope. Thus (3.4) says that at every nonleaf vertex vv other than the root, Dv​FD_{v}F is the sum of the slopes below vv, and that the slopes below the root sum to zero. Induction from the leaves proves the first identity in (3.7), and the condition at the root gives the second. Hence

∥Dv​F∥≤2​L​min⁡{|Cv|,m−|Cv|}≤2​L​⌊m/2⌋.\lVert D_{v}F\rVert\leq 2L\min\{|C_{v}|,m-|C_{v}|\}\leq 2L\lfloor m/2\rfloor.

The same arguments apply when some nonroot vertices have a single child (which may happen when we need to divide some edges). ∎

3.2. Definition of retraction in Theorem 1.1

Given a nonempty finite set A⊂XA\subset X, where XX is a normed space, let FAF_{A} be the harmonic interpolation on the tree TAT_{A} with boundary value aa at each leaf a∈Aa\in A. For 0≤s≤h⁡(root)0\leq s\leq h(\mathrm{root}), let pa​(s)p_{a}(s) be the ancestor of aa at height ss, and define

(3.8) rk​(A)={FA​(pa​(sk​(A))):a∈A}.r_{k}(A)=\{F_{A}(p_{a}(s_{k}(A))):a\in A\}.

For a singleton this means the same singleton. The formula defines rkr_{k} on all nonempty finite subsets of XX; the retraction in Theorem 1.1 is its restriction to X⁡(n)X(n). There are at most kk distinct cut points pa​(sk​(A))p_{a}(s_{k}(A)), so the output has at most kk points. If |A|≤k|A|\leq k, then sk​(A)=0s_{k}(A)=0 and rk​(A)=Ar_{k}(A)=A. Convex-hull preservation follows from the formula (3.5) expressing FF in terms of harmonic measure. By (3.2)–(3.3) we may apply Lemma 3.1 with L=(n−1)/2L=(n-1)/2 when A∈X⁡(n)A\in X(n); then (3.6) proves (1.1). It remains to prove the Lipschitz property of rkr_{k}.

3.3. Comparing two harmonic interpolations

We now compare harmonic interpolations on one tree for two choices of heights and boundary vectors. The difference is controlled by the changes of vertex heights; edge lengths, being differences of heights, do not enter separately.

Let TT be a finite rooted tree with leaves a1,…,ama_{1},\ldots,a_{m}, in which nonroot vertices may have a single child. A height function on TT is a function hh on its vertices that vanishes at the leaves and satisfies h⁡(v)≤h⁡(p⁡(v))h(v)\leq h(p(v)) for every nonroot vertex vv, so that the edge above vv has length ℓv=h⁡(p⁡(v))−h⁡(v)≥0\ell_{v}=h(p(v))-h(v)\geq 0. Lengths zero occur in the proof of Lemma 3.3, at the finitely many times where the single-linkage tree changes or points merge. If some lengths vanish, the harmonic interpolation of boundary vectors xix_{i} is defined on the tree obtained by contracting the edges of length zero, provided xi=xjx_{i}=x_{j} whenever aia_{i} and aja_{j} are contracted to the same vertex; each vertex of TT receives the value at its image. Leaf slopes are then defined as follows. If ℓai>0\ell_{a_{i}}>0, put qi=Dai​Fq_{i}=D_{a_{i}}F. Otherwise let uu be the highest ancestor of aia_{i} with h⁡(u)=0h(u)=0, whose subtree is contracted to a leaf, and put qi=Du​F/|Cu|q_{i}=D_{u}F/|C_{u}|, or qi=0q_{i}=0 if uu is the root. The identities (3.7) in the contracted tree give

(3.9) ∑i∈Cvqi=Dv​Fwhenever ​ℓv>0,∑iqi=0.\sum_{i\in C_{v}}q_{i}=D_{v}F\quad\text{whenever }\ell_{v}>0,\qquad\sum_{i}q_{i}=0.

Let hh and h′h^{\prime} be height functions on TT such that all edge lengths ℓv\ell_{v} for hh are positive. Lemma 3.3 (Moving points).

Lemma 3.4 (Common image).

Let A,B⊂XA,B\subset X be finite sets with dH​(A,B)≤εd_{H}(A,B)\leq\varepsilon. There are maps f:A→Xf\colon A\to X and g:B→Xg\colon B\to X such that f⁡(A)=g⁡(B)f(A)=g(B) and for all a∈Aa\in A and b∈Bb\in B we have ∥f⁡(a)−a∥≤ε\lVert f(a)-a\rVert\leq\varepsilon and ∥g⁡(b)−b∥≤ε\lVert g(b)-b\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

Proof.

Consider relations R⊂A×BR\subset A\times B such that a​R​baRb implies ∥a−b∥≤ε\lVert a-b\rVert\leq\varepsilon, every point of AA is related to some point of BB, and every point of BB is related to some point of AA. Choose such an RR with as few pairs as possible. If a​R​baRb, then aa and bb cannot both be related to other points, since otherwise the pair (a,b)(a,b) could be removed from RR. For a​R​baRb, put c⁡(a,b)=ac(a,b)=a if aa is related to more than one point, and c⁡(a,b)=bc(a,b)=b otherwise. By the preceding observation, c⁡(a,b)=bc(a,b)=b whenever bb is related to more than one point. Hence c⁡(a,b)=c⁡(a,b′)c(a,b)=c(a,b^{\prime}) whenever a​R​baRb and a​R​b′aRb^{\prime}, and c⁡(a,b)=c⁡(a′,b)c(a,b)=c(a^{\prime},b) whenever a​R​baRb and a′​R​ba^{\prime}Rb. Thus f⁡(a)=c⁡(a,b)f(a)=c(a,b) and g⁡(b)=c⁡(a,b)g(b)=c(a,b), for a​R​baRb, define maps on AA and on BB, both with image C={c⁡(a,b):a​R​b}C=\{c(a,b):aRb\}. They move points by at most ε\varepsilon, since c⁡(a,b)∈{a,b}c(a,b)\in\{a,b\}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Let A,B∈X⁡(n)A,B\in X(n) and ε=dH​(A,B)\varepsilon=d_{H}(A,B). Let ff, gg, and C=f⁡(A)=g⁡(B)C=f(A)=g(B) be as in Lemma 3.4. Since |A|,|B|≤n|A|,|B|\leq n, Lemma 3.3 applied to ff and to gg gives

dH​(rk​(A),rk​(B))≤dH​(rk​(A),rk​(C))+dH​(rk​(C),rk​(B))≤2​(1+4​n​(n−1))​ε=Dn​ε.d_{H}(r_{k}(A),r_{k}(B))\leq d_{H}(r_{k}(A),r_{k}(C))+d_{H}(r_{k}(C),r_{k}(B))\leq 2\bigl(1+4n(n-1)\bigr)\varepsilon=D_{n}\varepsilon.

The retraction, convex-hull, and movement assertions were proved after (3.8). ∎

4. Clustering by collision: proof of Theorem 1.2

We first outline the construction of a retraction X⁡(n)→X⁡(n−1)X(n)\to X(n-1). Embed XX linearly and isometrically into ℓ∞​(BX∗)\ell^{\infty}(B_{X^{*}}). Given an nn-point set AA, apply the proximal map of the convex function (4.2) coordinatewise at a scale chosen so that the closest pair(s) of points collide in every coordinate at once. The output is 11-Lipschitz with respect to the input and (n−1)(n-1)-Lipschitz with respect to the scale; however, it need not lie in the image of XX. Therefore, each point xx is replaced by a convex combination of the points of AA, with weights decreasing in the distance to xx. This step contributes the logarithmic factor in (1.2).

4.1. Separation and matching

This short subsection borrows from [1, Lemmas 2.5 and 2.6].

Definition 4.1.

The separation of A∈X⁡(n)A\in X(n) is

(4.1) δn​(A)={mina,b∈A,a≠b⁡d⁡(a,b),|A|=n,0,|A|<n.\delta_{n}(A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}a,b\in A,\ a\neq b\end{subarray}}d(a,b),&|A|=n,\\[4.0pt] 0,&|A|<n.\end{cases}
Lemma 4.2.

Let A,B∈X⁡(n)A,B\in X(n) and ε=dH​(A,B)\varepsilon=d_{H}(A,B). Then (a) |δn​(A)−δn​(B)|≤2​ε|\delta_{n}(A)-\delta_{n}(B)|\leq 2\varepsilon; (b) if max⁡{δn​(A),δn​(B)}>2​ε\max\{\delta_{n}(A),\delta_{n}(B)\}>2\varepsilon, then both sets have nn points and admit enumerations A={a1,…,an}A=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\} and B={b1,…,bn}B=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\} such that d⁡(ai,bi)≤εd(a_{i},b_{i})\leq\varepsilon for all ii.

Proof.

If max⁡{δn​(A),δn​(B)}≤2​ε\max\{\delta_{n}(A),\delta_{n}(B)\}\leq 2\varepsilon, then (a) is trivial. Suppose that δn​(A)>2​ε\delta_{n}(A)>2\varepsilon. For each a∈Aa\in A, choose a point of BB within distance ε\varepsilon. Distinct points of AA must have distinct choices, so |B|=n|B|=n and these choices give a bijection required by (b). Under this bijection every pairwise distance changes by at most 2​ε2\varepsilon, which implies (a). ∎

4.2. The proximal map

The map PtP_{t} used below is the scalar, equal-weight case of the convex-fusion clustering objective studied in [8]. To define it, fix n≥2n\geq 2 and set

(4.2) Ψ⁡(u)=∑1≤i<j≤n|ui−uj|,u∈ℝn.\Psi(u)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}|u_{i}-u_{j}|,\qquad u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

For t≥0t\geq 0 and a∈ℝna\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, define

(4.3) Pt​(a)=arg​minu∈ℝn⁡{12​∑i=1n(ui−ai)2+t​Ψ​(u)}.P_{t}(a)=\argmin_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(u_{i}-a_{i})^{2}+t\Psi(u)\right\}.

The objective function in (4.3) is coercive and strictly convex, so its minimizer exists and is unique. In particular, P0P_{0} is the identity. Permuting the coordinates of aa permutes those of Pt​(a)P_{t}(a) in the same way.

Lemma 4.3.

For all a,b∈ℝna,b\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and t,s≥0t,s\geq 0,

(4.4) ∥Pt​(a)−Ps​(b)∥∞\displaystyle\lVert P_{t}(a)-P_{s}(b)\rVert_{\infty} ≤∥a−b∥∞+(n−1)​|t−s|,\displaystyle\leq\lVert a-b\rVert_{\infty}+(n-1)|t-s|,
(4.5) ∥Pt​(a)−a∥∞\displaystyle\lVert P_{t}(a)-a\rVert_{\infty} ≤(n−1)​t.\displaystyle\leq(n-1)t.

Moreover, for every i,ji,j,

(4.6) |ai−aj|≤2​t⟹(Pt​(a))i=(Pt​(a))j.|a_{i}-a_{j}|\leq 2t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(P_{t}(a))_{i}=(P_{t}(a))_{j}.
Proof.

Write u=Pt​(a)u=P_{t}(a), and let Φ\Phi be the objective in (4.3). For w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the one-sided directional derivative

Φ′​(u,w)=limθ→0+Φ⁡(u+θ​w)−Φ⁡(u)θ\Phi^{\prime}(u;w)=\lim_{\theta\to 0^{+}}\frac{\Phi(u+\theta w)-\Phi(u)}{\theta}

exists since Φ\Phi is convex, and Φ′​(u,w)≥0\Phi^{\prime}(u;w)\geq 0 since uu is a minimizer.

For (4.6), suppose that ui<uju_{i}<u_{j}, and let w=ei−ejw=e_{i}-e_{j}. The term |ui−uj||u_{i}-u_{j}| contributes −2-2 to Ψ′​(u,w)\Psi^{\prime}(u;w). For l∉{i,j}l\notin\{i,j\}, the terms |ui−ul||u_{i}-u_{l}| and |ul−uj||u_{l}-u_{j}| contribute ±1\pm 1 each, with +1+1 only if ui≥ulu_{i}\geq u_{l}, respectively ul≥uju_{l}\geq u_{j}. Since ui<uju_{i}<u_{j}, at most one of them is +1+1. Hence Ψ′​(u,w)≤−2\Psi^{\prime}(u;w)\leq-2, and

0≤Φ′​(u,w)≤(ui−ai)−(uj−aj)−2​t,0\leq\Phi^{\prime}(u;w)\leq(u_{i}-a_{i})-(u_{j}-a_{j})-2t,

that is, aj−ai≥2​t+(uj−ui)>2​ta_{j}-a_{i}\geq 2t+(u_{j}-u_{i})>2t. Interchanging ii and jj proves (4.6).

For (4.4), let v=Ps​(b)v=P_{s}(b), let Φ~\tilde{\Phi} be the objective defining vv, and put

M=maxi⁡(ui−vi),E={i:ui−vi=M}.M=\max_{i}(u_{i}-v_{i}),\qquad E=\{i:u_{i}-v_{i}=M\}.

Let 𝟏E\boldsymbol{1}_{E} be the indicator vector of EE. The quadratic terms of Φ′​(u,−𝟏E)\Phi^{\prime}(u;-\boldsymbol{1}_{E}) and Φ~′​(v,𝟏E)\tilde{\Phi}^{\prime}(v;\boldsymbol{1}_{E}) add up to −∑i∈E(M−(ai−bi))-\sum_{i\in E}\bigl(M-(a_{i}-b_{i})\bigr). In Ψ\Psi, only the terms with i∈Ei\in E and j∉Ej\notin E contribute. Such a term |ui−uj||u_{i}-u_{j}| contributes tt times ±1\pm 1, with +1+1 only if ui≤uju_{i}\leq u_{j}, and the corresponding term |vi−vj||v_{i}-v_{j}| contributes ss times ±1\pm 1, with +1+1 only if vi≥vjv_{i}\geq v_{j}. Since ui−uj>vi−vju_{i}-u_{j}>v_{i}-v_{j}, at most one of them is +1+1, so together they contribute at most |t−s||t-s|. There are at most |E|​(n−1)|E|(n-1) such pairs. Adding Φ′​(u,−𝟏E)≥0\Phi^{\prime}(u;-\boldsymbol{1}_{E})\geq 0 and Φ~′​(v,𝟏E)≥0\tilde{\Phi}^{\prime}(v;\boldsymbol{1}_{E})\geq 0 therefore gives

|E|​M≤∑i∈E(ai−bi)+|E|(n−1)|t−s|≤|E|(∥a−b∥∞+(n−1)​|t−s|).|E|M\leq\sum_{i\in E}(a_{i}-b_{i})+|E|(n-1)|t-s|\leq|E|\bigl(\lVert a-b\rVert_{\infty}+(n-1)|t-s|\bigr).

Interchanging (a,t)(a,t) and (b,s)(b,s) proves (4.4). Finally, (4.5) is the case b=ab=a, s=0s=0 of (4.4), since P0P_{0} is the identity. ∎

4.3. Coordinatewise collision

Let Γ\Gamma be any nonempty index set and V=ℓ∞​(Γ)V=\ell^{\infty}(\Gamma). For the rest of the section the vector norms are ℓ∞\ell^{\infty} norms. For an ordered tuple x=(x1,…,xn)∈Vnx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in V^{n}, define 𝒫t​(x)=(y1,…,yn)\mathcal{P}_{t}(x)=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) coordinatewise by

(4.7) (y1​(γ),…,yn​(γ))=Pt​(x1​(γ),…,xn​(γ)),γ∈Γ.\bigl(y_{1}(\gamma),\ldots,y_{n}(\gamma)\bigr)=P_{t}\bigl(x_{1}(\gamma),\ldots,x_{n}(\gamma)\bigr),\qquad\gamma\in\Gamma.

By (4.5), the yiy_{i} are bounded functions. Lemma 4.3 implies

(4.8) maxi⁡∥yi−xi∥\displaystyle\max_{i}\lVert y_{i}-x_{i}\rVert ≤(n−1)​t,\displaystyle\leq(n-1)t,
(4.9) maxi⁡∥𝒫t​(x)i−𝒫s​(x′)i∥\displaystyle\max_{i}\lVert\mathcal{P}_{t}(x)_{i}-\mathcal{P}_{s}(x^{\prime})_{i}\rVert ≤maxi⁡∥xi−xi′∥+(n−1)​|t−s|.\displaystyle\leq\max_{i}\lVert x_{i}-x^{\prime}_{i}\rVert+(n-1)|t-s|.

(4.10) ∥xi−xj∥≤2​t⟹yi=yj.\lVert x_{i}-x_{j}\rVert\leq 2t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_{i}=y_{j}.

We will use the above properties of 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} to obtain convex-hull-preserving retractions X⁡(n)→X⁡(n−1)X(n)\to X(n-1) in a general normed space XX. Toward that, recall that XX embeds linearly and isometrically into VV for some index set Γ\Gamma, e.g., Γ=BX∗\Gamma=B_{X^{*}}. Thus, we consider XX to be a (not necessarily closed) subspace of VV.

c=n−12,b=3​n−12,λ=log⁡(n+1)n,c=\frac{n-1}{2},\quad b=\frac{3n-1}{2},\quad\lambda=\frac{\log(n+1)}{n},

φ⁡(r)=eλ​(b−r)+−1,r≥0.\varphi(r)=e^{\lambda(b-r)^{+}}-1,\quad r\geq 0.

The map TsT_{s} commutes with permutations of the labels and satisfies

(4.21) ∑j|wjW−wj′W′|≤2max⁡{W,W′}​∑j|wj−wj′|.\sum_{j}\Bigl|\frac{w_{j}}{W}-\frac{w^{\prime}_{j}}{W^{\prime}}\Bigr|\leq\frac{2}{\max\{W,W^{\prime}\}}\sum_{j}\lvert w_{j}-w^{\prime}_{j}\rvert.

If wi​j′>0w^{\prime}_{ij}>0, then likewise ∥xj′−xi′∥<(2​n−1)​s′\lVert x^{\prime}_{j}-x^{\prime}_{i}\rVert<(2n-1)s^{\prime}, so ∥xj−xi∥<(2​n−1)​s+2​ε<2​n​s\lVert x_{j}-x_{i}\rVert<(2n-1)s+2\varepsilon<2ns. Ts​(x)i−Ts′​(x′)i=∑j(pi​j−pi​j′)​(xj−xi)+∑jpi​j′​(xj−xj′),T_{s}(x)_{i}-T_{s^{\prime}}(x^{\prime})_{i}=\sum_{j}(p_{ij}-p^{\prime}_{ij})(x_{j}-x_{i})+\sum_{j}p^{\prime}_{ij}(x_{j}-x^{\prime}_{j}),

and (4.22) gives

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Set rn​(A)=Ar_{n}(A)=A when |A|<n|A|<n. If A={x1,…,xn}A=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}, put

rn​(A)={Tδn​(A)​(x)1,…,Tδn​(A)​(x)n}.r_{n}(A)=\{T_{\delta_{n}(A)}(x)_{1},\ldots,T_{\delta_{n}(A)}(x)_{n}\}.

This is independent of the enumeration. A pair realizing δn​(A)\delta_{n}(A) collides by (4.15), so the set rn​(A)r_{n}(A) has at most n−1n-1 points. It lies in the convex hull of AA and satisfies

(4.23) dH​(rn​(A),A)≤(2​n−1)​δn​(A).d_{H}(r_{n}(A),A)\leq(2n-1)\delta_{n}(A).

Let ε=dH​(A,B)\varepsilon=d_{H}(A,B). If max⁡(δn​(A),δn​(B))≤2​ε\max(\delta_{n}(A),\delta_{n}(B))\leq 2\varepsilon, inequality (4.23) yields

dH​(rn​(A),rn​(B))≤(8​n−3)​ε≤Cn​ε.d_{H}(r_{n}(A),r_{n}(B))\leq(8n-3)\varepsilon\leq C_{n}\varepsilon.

Otherwise Lemma 4.2 gives enumerations of the two nn-point sets with matching distances at most ε\varepsilon, and |δn​(A)−δn​(B)|≤2​ε|\delta_{n}(A)-\delta_{n}(B)|\leq 2\varepsilon. Applying (4.16) to these enumerations with s=δn​(A)s=\delta_{n}(A) and s′=δn​(B)s^{\prime}=\delta_{n}(B) yields Lip⁡(rn)≤Cn\Lip(r_{n})\leq C_{n}.

The 11-Lipschitz property of the midpoint retraction X⁡(2)→X⁡(1)X(2)\to X(1) is straightforward. ∎

The following is a corollary of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2.

Corollary 4.5.

Recall the constants Bn,kB_{n,k} from (1.3). For 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, every nonempty convex subset YY of any normed space admits a Bn,kB_{n,k}-Lipschitz retraction rn,k:Y⁡(n)→Y⁡(k)r_{n,k}\colon Y(n)\to Y(k) whose output lies in the convex hull of the input.

5. Clustering via barycenters: proof of Theorem 1.3

Let 𝒫fin​(X)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X) denote the space of finitely supported probability measures on a nonempty metric space XX, equipped with the 11-Wasserstein distance

W1​(μ,ν)=infπ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)∫X×Xd⁡(x,y)​𝑑π​(x,y),W_{1}(\mu,\nu)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y),

where Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) is the set of couplings of μ,ν\mu,\nu.

Definition 5.1.

A KK-Lipschitz barycenter on XX is a map β:𝒫fin​(X)→X\beta\colon\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X)\to X such that

(5.1) β⁡(δx)=x,d⁡(β⁡(μ),β⁡(ν))≤K​W1​(μ,ν).\beta(\delta_{x})=x,\qquad d(\beta(\mu),\beta(\nu))\leq KW_{1}(\mu,\nu).

Here δx\delta_{x} is the Dirac probability measure at xx; it is unrelated to the separation δn\delta_{n} from Definition 4.1. In the terminology of Mendel and Naor [15], the existence of such a map β\beta means that XX is W1W_{1}-barycentric with constant KK.

Lemma 5.2.

For every metric space XX, the space (𝒫fin​(X),W1)(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X),W_{1}) is isometric to a convex subset of a real normed space.

Proof.

Let ℳfin0​(X)\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X) be the vector space of finitely supported signed measures of total mass zero, with the Kantorovich–Rubinstein norm

‖η‖KR=supLip⁡(f)≤1|∫Xf​𝑑η|.\|\eta\|_{\mathrm{KR}}=\sup_{\Lip(f)\leq 1}\left|\int_{X}f\,d\eta\right|.

Put S=supp⁡μ∪supp⁡νS=\supp\mu\cup\supp\nu. Every 11-Lipschitz function f:S→ℝf\colon S\to\mathbb{R} extends to a 11-Lipschitz function on XX by the McShane–Whitney theorem. Thus the supremum defining ‖μ−ν‖KR\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{KR}} is unchanged if it is taken over 11-Lipschitz functions on SS. Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality [16, I.5, Case 5.16], applied to the finite metric space SS, therefore gives ‖μ−ν‖KR=W1​(μ,ν)\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{KR}}=W_{1}(\mu,\nu).

Fixing o∈Xo\in X, the map μ↦μ−δo\mu\mapsto\mu-\delta_{o} is an isometric affine embedding of 𝒫fin​(X)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X), with convex image. ∎

The completion of ℳfin0​(X)\mathcal{M}^{0}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X) is the Arens–Eells space of XX, also known as its Lipschitz-free space; see [17].

Theorem 5.3.

If a metric space XX admits a KK-Lipschitz barycenter on 𝒫fin​(X)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X), then, for every 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, there is a retraction r:X⁡(n)→X⁡(k)r\colon X(n)\to X(k) such that Lip⁡(r)≤K​Bn,k\Lip(r)\leq KB_{n,k}, with Bn,kB_{n,k} as in (1.3). It can be chosen to satisfy

(5.2) r(A)⊂{β(μ):μ∈𝒫fin(X),suppμ⊂A}.r(A)\subset\{\beta(\mu):\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X),\ \supp\mu\subset A\}.
Proof.

By Lemma 5.2 and Corollary 4.5, there is a retraction S:𝒫fin​(X)​(n)→𝒫fin​(X)​(k)S\colon\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X)(n)\to\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X)(k) with Lip⁡(S)≤Bn,k\Lip(S)\leq B_{n,k}, whose output lies in the convex hull of its input. The map ι:X⁡(n)→𝒫fin​(X)​(n)\iota\colon X(n)\to\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X)(n) given by ι⁡(A)={δx:x∈A}\iota(A)=\{\delta_{x}:x\in A\} is isometric, because W1​(δx,δy)=d⁡(x,y)W_{1}(\delta_{x},\delta_{y})=d(x,y). For A∈X⁡(n)A\in X(n), define r⁡(A)=β⁡(S⁡(ι⁡(A)))r(A)=\beta(S(\iota(A))). By construction, r⁡(A)r(A) has at most kk points. If |A|≤k|A|\leq k, then S⁡(ι⁡(A))=ι⁡(A)S(\iota(A))=\iota(A) and r⁡(A)=Ar(A)=A. The Lipschitz estimate follows by composition. Every measure in S⁡(ι⁡(A))S(\iota(A)) is a convex combination of the Dirac measures at points of AA, proving (5.2). ∎

Remark 5.4.

If XX admits a KK-Lipschitz barycenter β\beta, then the map r⁡({x,y})={β⁡((δx+δy)/2)}r(\{x,y\})=\{\beta((\delta_{x}+\delta_{y})/2)\} is easily seen to be a KK-Lipschitz retraction X⁡(2)→X⁡(1)X(2)\to X(1). For the usual vector barycenter in a normed space, this is the midpoint retraction.

Corollary 5.5.

For every metric space MM, the space (𝒫fin​(M),W1)(\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(M),W_{1}) satisfies Λn,k≤Bn,k\Lambda_{n,k}\leq B_{n,k} for all 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. If MM is Polish, the same conclusions hold for the space (𝒫1​(M),W1)(\mathcal{P}_{1}(M),W_{1}) of Borel probability measures with finite first moment.

Proof.

The first assertion follows directly from Lemma 5.2 and Corollary 4.5. For the second, use the vector space of finite signed Borel measures η\eta satisfying

η⁡(M)=0,∫Md⁡(o,x)​d​|η|​(x)<∞,\eta(M)=0,\qquad\int_{M}d(o,x)\,d|\eta|(x)<\infty,

with the same Kantorovich–Rubinstein norm. The duality formula for 𝒫1​(M)\mathcal{P}_{1}(M) [16, I.5, Case 5.16] shows that μ↦μ−δo\mu\mapsto\mu-\delta_{o} is an isometry with convex image. Apply Corollary 4.5 again. ∎

For example, (𝒫1​(S1),W1)(\mathcal{P}_{1}(S^{1}),W_{1}) has the Lipschitz clustering property, although S1S^{1} itself does not have it [12].

Definition 5.6.

[3, 6] A conical geodesic bicombing on a metric space XX assigns to each ordered pair x,y∈Xx,y\in X a constant-speed geodesic σx​y:[0,1]→X\sigma_{xy}\colon[0,1]\to X from xx to yy, such that

(5.3) d⁡(σx​y​(t),σx′​y′​(t))≤(1−t)​d​(x,x′)+t​d​(y,y′)(0≤t≤1).d(\sigma_{xy}(t),\sigma_{x^{\prime}y^{\prime}}(t))\leq(1-t)d(x,x^{\prime})+td(y,y^{\prime})\qquad(0\leq t\leq 1).

A subset of XX is σ\sigma-convex if it contains the selected geodesic between each pair of its points, and conv¯σ​A\overline{\conv}_{\sigma}A denotes the smallest closed σ\sigma-convex subset containing AA.

If XX is complete and admits a conical bicombing σ\sigma, then it admits a 11-Lipschitz barycenter β\beta on 𝒫fin​(X)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{fin}}(X) with β⁡(μ)∈conv¯σ​(supp⁡μ)\beta(\mu)\in\overline{\conv}_{\sigma}(\supp\mu). This is the finite-support part of [3, Theorems 2.6 and 2.7], where the barycenter is constructed on the space of Radon probability measures with finite first moment.

Corollary 5.7.

Every complete metric space XX with a conical geodesic bicombing satisfies Λn,k​(X)≤Bn,k\Lambda_{n,k}(X)\leq B_{n,k} for all 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. The retractions can be chosen so that r⁡(A)⊂conv¯σ​Ar(A)\subset\overline{\conv}_{\sigma}A. In particular, this applies to every complete Busemann-convex space, and hence to every Hadamard space.

Proof.

Apply Theorem 5.3 to the barycenter just described. Its property β⁡(μ)∈conv¯σ​(supp⁡μ)\beta(\mu)\in\overline{\conv}_{\sigma}(\supp\mu) gives the stated containment, and Remark 5.4 gives the two-point constant. In a Busemann-convex geodesic space, the distance between two constant-speed geodesics is convex, so its unique geodesics satisfy (5.3). ∎

Theorem 5.3, Remark 5.4, and Corollary 5.7 prove Theorem 1.3.

6. Absolute retracts, lower bounds, and open questions

The existence of retractions between finite subset spaces is inherited by Lipschitz retracts.

Lemma 6.1 ([2, Lemma 3.3]).

Let g:X→Zg\colon X\to Z and f:Z→Xf\colon Z\to X be Lipschitz maps with f∘g=idXf\circ g=\operatorname{id}_{X}. Then

Λn,k​(X)≤Lip⁡(f)​Lip⁡(g)​Λn,k​(Z)(1≤k<n).\Lambda_{n,k}(X)\leq\Lip(f)\Lip(g)\,\Lambda_{n,k}(Z)\qquad(1\leq k<n).
Proof.

Apply maps to finite sets pointwise. If R:Z⁡(n)→Z⁡(k)R\colon Z(n)\to Z(k) is a retraction, then f∘R∘gf\circ R\circ g is a retraction X⁡(n)→X⁡(k)X(n)\to X(k), and its Lipschitz constant is at most Lip⁡(f)​Lip⁡(R)​Lip​(g)\Lip(f)\Lip(R)\Lip(g). ∎

Definition 6.2.

A metric space XX is an absolute λ\lambda-Lipschitz retract if every isometric copy of XX in a metric space is the image of a λ\lambda-Lipschitz retraction.

For example, ℓ∞​(Γ)\ell^{\infty}(\Gamma) is an absolute 11-Lipschitz retract.

Corollary 6.3.

Every absolute λ\lambda-Lipschitz retract XX satisfies Λn,k​(X)≤λ⁡(2​n−1)\Lambda_{n,k}(X)\leq\lambda(2n-1) for 1≤k<n1\leq k<n.

Proof.

For a fixed o∈Xo\in X, the map x↦d⁡(x,⋅)−d⁡(o,⋅)x\mapsto d(x,\cdot)-d(o,\cdot) embeds XX isometrically into ℓ∞​(X)\ell^{\infty}(X), so XX is a λ\lambda-Lipschitz retract of ℓ∞​(X)\ell^{\infty}(X). Apply Theorem 2.3 and Lemma 6.1. ∎

The constants in Theorems 1.1, 1.2, and 2.3 grow with nn, and some growth is unavoidable.

Proposition 6.4.

Let XX contain an isometric copy of a nondegenerate interval. Then Λn​(X)≥n−3\Lambda_{n}(X)\geq n-3 for all n≥2n\geq 2.

Proof.

For an interval [0,L][0,L], this is [2, Theorem 5.1]. Let c:[0,L]→Xc\colon[0,L]\to X be an isometry. The map f⁡(x)=min⁡{L,d⁡(x,c⁡(0))}f(x)=\min\{L,d(x,c(0))\} is 11-Lipschitz and satisfies f∘c=idf\circ c=\operatorname{id}, so Lemma 6.1 gives Λn​([0,L])≤Λn​(X)\Lambda_{n}([0,L])\leq\Lambda_{n}(X). ∎

Question 6.5.

Is Λn​(X)=O​(n)\Lambda_{n}(X)=O(n) for every normed space XX?

Question 6.6.

Is sup1≤k<nΛn,k​(X)=O⁡(n)\sup_{1\leq k<n}\Lambda_{n,k}(X)=O(n) for every normed space XX?

For normed spaces of dimension at least two, the lower bound also grows with the size of the target: Λn,k​(X)≥k/(2​π)−1/2\Lambda_{n,k}(X)\geq k/(2\pi)-1/2 by [2, Theorem 1.1].
